module_title: VPC Networking, Address Planning and Routing
review_basis: Individually inspected original SAP Module 04 numbered WebPs 17–20; script follows their global-core architecture, PrivateLink flows and side-by-side connectivity comparison.
part_title: Cloud WAN, PrivateLink and Connectivity Architecture Choices

scenes.title: Cloud WAN: policy-driven global core
scenes.visual_overview: The central Cloud WAN core connects regional core network edges under one global policy, with production, development and shared segments on both sides.
visual_walkthrough: Start at the core network policy box defining segments, routing behavior, and attachment mapping
Follow the dotted links from the global core toward both regional core network edges
Trace the production, development, and shared attachments in each Region, including on-premises VPN attachments
Compare regional Transit Gateway routing with Cloud WAN's centrally managed multi-Region core and the explicit segment-sharing caveat
scenes.visual_example: An enterprise with production and development VPCs and on-premises branches across US and EU Regions uses Cloud WAN segment policies instead of assuming automatic connectivity between all networks.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Choose Cloud WAN for centrally governed multi-Region networking; connectivity between isolated segments requires deliberate policy and routing.
scenes.narration: This diagram is about making a global network manageable without treating every VPC as one flat network. Begin at the center: AWS Cloud WAN supplies a global core network, with a core network policy above it. That policy defines segments, maps attachments, and controls routing behavior. Follow the dotted connections outward to the regional core network edges in the US-East and EU-West examples. Each edge receives attachments from production, development, and shared VPC environments, while on-premises sites can join through VPN attachments. Notice how the same logical segments appear in both Regions. This enables central governance of a multi-Region design, but it does not mean that production and development can automatically communicate. The orange caveat box is essential: route sharing across segments needs explicit policy and applicable attachments. Now compare the bottom panels. A Transit Gateway is a regional routing hub with attachment route tables. Cloud WAN is useful when many Regions, accounts, and networks need a centrally administered policy model. For an exam scenario, prefer Cloud WAN for policy-driven global connectivity; use Transit Gateway when a regional hub is sufficient. Always inspect effective segment policy and routing before diagnosing a connectivity failure.

scenes.title: PrivateLink: a private service without VPC peering
scenes.visual_overview: The consumer application reaches one provider service across PrivateLink even though both VPCs display the same overlapping CIDR.
visual_walkthrough: Point out the overlapping 10.10.0.0/16 addresses on consumer and provider VPCs
Follow consumer application to interface endpoint ENI and across the AWS private network path
Trace the provider Network Load Balancer forwarding to application targets
Explain allowed principals, endpoint acceptance, endpoint security groups, and endpoint processing charges
scenes.visual_example: A consumer VPC and SaaS provider VPC both use 10.10.0.0/16; PrivateLink still exposes only the published provider service, unlike peering.
scenes.visual_synthesis: PrivateLink grants private service-level access, not VPC-to-VPC routed reachability or transitive networking.
scenes.narration: The key idea on this slide is private access to one service, not a network connection between two VPCs. Look at the CIDR labels first. Both the consumer VPC and provider VPC use ten dot ten dot zero dot zero slash sixteen. Those overlapping ranges prevent ordinary routed peering, but PrivateLink does not require the two VPC networks to exchange routes. Follow the orange arrow from the consumer application into an interface VPC endpoint. That endpoint creates private network interfaces in the selected subnets. Traffic then traverses the AWS private network to the provider's endpoint service, backed in this example by a Network Load Balancer. The load balancer forwards requests to the application targets. The three bottom boxes are important operational controls. The provider authorizes allowed principals and can require acceptance of endpoint connections. The consumer secures the interface endpoint with appropriate security group rules. And neither side gets unrestricted reachability to the other's VPC; only the advertised service is exposed. PrivateLink carries hourly endpoint and data-processing charges. Choose this pattern when a consumer needs a specific internal API or SaaS service, especially where CIDRs overlap or full-network connectivity would be excessive.

scenes.title: PrivateLink provider setup: NLB to endpoint service
scenes.visual_overview: The picture expands the previous service access design into configuration steps and a request path from consumer DNS to multi-AZ provider targets.
visual_walkthrough: Start at the client resolving the endpoint service DNS or verified private DNS
Trace interface endpoints in selected Availability Zones and the associated endpoint security group
Inspect the endpoint service with allowed AWS account principals and optional manual acceptance
Follow the Network Load Balancer listeners and healthy targets in Availability Zones A, B and C
Review the bottom request-flow sequence and separate provider checks from consumer checks
scenes.visual_example: A provider publishes a TCP or TLS application behind an NLB in multiple Availability Zones; customers create interface endpoints and verify DNS, acceptance and connectivity.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A healthy NLB does not by itself guarantee access: endpoint acceptance, service DNS, client security groups and supported Availability Zones must also line up.
scenes.narration: Now we can configure the PrivateLink design rather than just recognize it. Begin on the left with the consumer client. It uses the service's endpoint DNS name, or a private DNS name when the provider has configured and verified that option. The client's request enters an interface endpoint, which creates endpoint network interfaces in the selected Availability Zones. The endpoint security group must permit the intended service traffic from consumer clients. Move to the purple center box: the provider creates an endpoint service associated with a Network Load Balancer, authorizes suitable account principals, and chooses whether connection requests require manual acceptance. Follow the orange arrow to the provider VPC. The NLB has a listener and target group for the service port, then distributes traffic to healthy targets across enabled Availability Zones. The horizontal sequence near the bottom restates the actual request path: client, interface endpoint, endpoint service, NLB, and healthy targets. For troubleshooting, separate the two responsibilities. On the provider side, check the NLB listener, target health, allowed principals and acceptance state. On the consumer side, verify endpoint state, DNS resolution and endpoint security group rules. A service can be healthy but still unreachable when any of these boundaries is wrong.

scenes.title: Choose peering, Transit Gateway or PrivateLink
scenes.visual_overview: Three architectural options are shown side by side, followed by a decision table comparing reachability, transitivity, CIDRs and typical use cases.
visual_walkthrough: Compare the left two-VPC peering diagram with direct nontransitive routing
Inspect the center Transit Gateway hub serving several VPCs plus hybrid connections, with route segmentation
Inspect right-side PrivateLink interface endpoint to one NLB-backed service and overlapping CIDR support
Read decision table by scope, network reachability, transitivity, CIDR requirements and key capability
Use the bottom scenario boxes to choose an option and finish with cost, security and DNS caveats
scenes.visual_example: Two VPCs that exchange protocols choose peering; many VPCs plus on-premises routing choose TGW; a SaaS API consumed from an overlapping VPC chooses PrivateLink.
scenes.visual_synthesis: First ask whether the consumer needs a direct network link, a routed hub, or only one exposed service; then validate CIDR, routing, cost, security and DNS constraints.
scenes.narration: This is a decision slide, so the three columns are alternatives rather than steps in a single traffic flow. In the left column, VPC peering connects two nonoverlapping VPC networks directly. Applications can use many protocols, but peering is nontransitive: one peer cannot serve as an intermediary to another VPC. In the middle, AWS Transit Gateway acts as a regional hub connecting multiple VPCs and hybrid networks. Its attachments and route tables provide centrally controlled routing and segmentation, but you still need appropriate subnet routes and security controls. In the right column, AWS PrivateLink gives a consumer an interface endpoint to a particular provider service behind a Network Load Balancer. It does not route the consumer into the provider's entire VPC, and overlapping address space is possible. Look at the comparison table underneath. Focus on scope, network-level reachability, transitivity, CIDR requirements and operational purpose. Now apply the three scenarios at the bottom. Two VPCs exchanging several protocols often fit peering. Dozens of VPCs plus on-premises routing usually justify Transit Gateway. A SaaS provider publishing one API to a customer with an overlapping CIDR fits PrivateLink. Finally, use the caveat row: pricing, segmentation, endpoint policy and DNS can change an otherwise sensible choice. The exam decision begins with one question: do you need an entire network, a routing hub, or only a service?
